turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, Mrs Pillay is in. I did the lying and standing blood pressures while you were finishing next door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Sister. Mrs Pillay, come through. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. My daughter insisted. She reckons I fell.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me in your own words what happened.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I didn't really fall. I slid down. Twice. It's not the same thing.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Slid down. Where were you?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): First time I was in the kitchen, reaching for a cup. My knees went and I just sat on the floor, sort of. Second time was by the bed.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And when was the kitchen one?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Um. I don't know, doctor. Last week? Or the week before that. The days run together.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, we won't force a date. The one by the bed?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Yesterday morning. I'd just stood up. I slid onto the carpet. My daughter heard the thud, shame, and came running.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you hurt yourself? Bang your head at all?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No, no bang on the head. There's a small bruise on the hip, but it's nothing, really.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about dizziness?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, when I stand up the head goes light. Few seconds. If I hold the cupboard it passes.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every time you get up?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Mostly mornings. Not every time. I don't know, doctor, I haven't counted.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when it happens?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the breathing?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): I get a bit puffed walking to the gate. That's been there for ages, it's not new. Not while I'm dizzy.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart racing, palpitations?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blacking out, or weakness down one side, or the words not coming?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No blackouts. No weakness. I was awake the whole time. I told her it wasn't a proper fall.

[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, her daughter caught me in the passage. She says she found her on the floor both times, and the second time Mrs Pillay was out for a moment and didn't answer.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): I wasn't out. I don't know why she says that. I was looking at her.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'm hearing two stories and I won't pick a winner yet. I'm not going to call this a blackout, and I'm not calling it a stroke. It might be the pressure falling when you stand, or the tablets, or you being a bit dry, so we'll see what fits.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sister, can you read me those pressures?

[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Lying, one hundred and fifty two over eighty eight, pulse seventy four. Standing at three minutes, one hundred and eighteen over seventy two, pulse ninety six. She felt woozy during the stand.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a proper drop. How are you feeling sitting now?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine sitting. It's the getting up.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): What blood pressure tablets are you on?

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, the white one, ten milligrams in the morning. Perindopril four milligrams, also morning. And the water tablet, hydrochloro... hydrochlorothiazide, I think twelve point five milligrams.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): You think. Do you take that one every day?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Maybe three times a week. It makes me rush to the toilet and I'm scared I'll slip again. I don't know if I should have been doing that, doctor.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): And for sleep?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Zolpidem, ten milligrams at night. My daughter gets cross, so some nights I skip it. I couldn't tell you how many.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else from the chemist? Aspirin, something for sugar?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): No aspirin, no sugar tablets. There's a vitamin in the cupboard but I don't even know the name. It's not important.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any medicine that doesn't agree with you, allergies?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Penicillin, maybe, when I was small. My mother said I came out in a rash. I've kept away from it ever since.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just a rash, or did you swell up, struggle to breathe?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't remember swelling. Just the rash, I think. It was so long ago.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Other illnesses? Diabetes, a stroke, heart trouble?
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, that's the one. No diabetes. No stroke. My husband had a heart attack, but he passed, what, eight years back.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry to hear that. Do you still smoke? A drink in the evening?
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): I gave up cigarettes years ago. A glass of wine with Sunday lunch, that's me. I stay with my daughter in Plumstead. She fusses.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh, and the medical aid card is in her bag, I hope she didn't leave it in the car. Sorry, that's not your problem.

[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll sort the card later. Let me look at you: grip is equal in both hands, no droop of the face, heart is regular and the chest is clear. That hip bruise is small and there's no tenderness on the bone.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): See. Nothing broken.

[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): The drop in pressure when you stand fits the light head, and my working thought is postural hypotension, nudged along by the tablets. Dehydration is still possible, and I'm not closing the door on an inner-ear balance problem either, so that stays on the list. I am not diagnosing a stroke today.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): So it's the tablets?

[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's the leading idea, not a final label. I'm going to stop the hydrochlorothiazide. It can pull the pressure down, and taking it on and off isn't helping us. Carry on with amlodipine ten milligrams and perindopril four milligrams every morning.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Stop the water one completely? I don't know, doctor, won't the pressure shoot up?
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll keep an eye on it. I'd like bloods before you go, urea and electrolytes and a full blood count. Sister can take them on the way out.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): Ja, I'll do them just now.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the dizziness hasn't settled in two weeks, we might organise a brain scan. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): A scan. Alright. I hope it's a waste of time.

[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks either way, and we'll repeat the standing pressure. If you slide down again before then, or someone can't wake you properly, don't sit on it, come straight to casualty.
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks. She'll bring me. She already thinks I'm worse than I am.

[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): She's being careful, and that's allowed. When you stand, do it slowly, hold on, and the zolpidem stays ten milligrams only on nights you truly can't sleep. No water tablet from today.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

omissions.text: Patient denied blacking out/loss of consciousness and said she was awake the whole time.
Patient denied speech difficulty ('the words not coming').
Breathlessness is not new and does not occur during the dizzy episodes.
Standing blood pressure and pulse were measured at three minutes, and she felt woozy during the stand.
Hydrochlorothiazide was being taken only about three times a week because it made her rush to the toilet and she was scared of slipping again.
No aspirin and no diabetes/sugar tablets.
When asked about penicillin allergy severity, patient did not recall swelling or breathing difficulty, only rash.
Patient denied heart trouble/history of heart disease.
Doctor explicitly said he was not calling this a blackout and was not diagnosing a stroke today.
Doctor advised to continue amlodipine 10 mg every morning and perindopril 4 mg every morning.
Planned blood tests were to be taken before she left that day, with nurse to do them on the way out/just now.
